source.title_on_document: Generative AI Enhances Team Performance and Reduces Need for Traditional Teams

supplement.where: Supplementary Materials on OSF: https://osf.io/zq48w/?view_only=ca644891d4234935b1464fbc20ce6e85 (p. 8, footnote 3). Preregistration: https://osf.io/5su8c/?view_only=24f9efec395c4581b880e7773792d23d (p. 4, footnote 1).
supplement.holds: Lab setting, task details, rating scale for judges, post-experiment questionnaire items, and the method for the GPT-scored human-input measure (pp. 8, 10, 19). All regression tables with robust standard errors and the descriptive tables with arm means and SDs are in Appendices A and B of this PDF.

paper_design_summary: Experiment I: 435 lab participants (working professionals and college students) were randomly allocated to 122 teams of three to five, and teams were randomly assigned to human-only, single-AI (one ChatGPT-4 touchpoint per team), or multiple-AI (one ChatGPT-4 touchpoint per member) conditions; each team wrote a series of articles on college job hunting and a digital-transformation strategy for a retail chain. Blind online judges (six per output) rated each output 1-10 on overall quality, novelty, and usefulness. Experiment II recruited 139 separate individuals who each did the same two tasks with ChatGPT-4, and compared them with the Experiment I teams without random assignment.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The analysis dataset 'comprised 244 observational samples from 122 teams, each completing two tasks' (pp. 10-11), i.e. every randomized team, so all 435 participants (142/150/143) are in the performance analysis; Appendix A Table 1 lists 42/41/39 teams, and mean team size x teams reproduces 142/150/143. Completion-time regressions use N = 235 (p. 43, Table 7); process-perception regressions N = 122 teams.

ai_tool.how_used: Teams used ChatGPT-4.0 freely while completing the tasks; chat logs were extracted for mechanism analysis. Single-AI teams shared one touchpoint; multiple-AI teams had one per member.

task.description: Two professional tasks done by each team: (1) content generation, writing a series of in-depth articles on college students' job hunting and career development; (2) strategy development, a digital transformation strategy for a traditional retail chain. The paper says the tasks entail content creation, innovation, and strategic thinking. Task type mixes creative writing and business-idea generation.

outcomes.measure_detail: Online panel of judges blind to hypotheses and conditions; six independent raters per output; 1-10 scale on overall quality (Amabile, 1983); Cronbach's alpha 0.759 (p. 10). Coded usefulness because the codebook puts 'quality' there; it is the paper's overall rating dimension. Per-task means also reported (Appendix A Table 1, Task1/Task2). Distributional comparison in Figure 5 (relative density, single vs multiple AI).

eligibility.reason: Experiment I randomly assigned 435 people (via 122 randomly formed teams; assignment is clustered by team) to ChatGPT-4 access (single or multiple touchpoints) or no AI, and blind judges rated each team's articles and strategy on overall quality, novelty, and usefulness. The tasks are content creation and strategy ideation rated on novelty, so they fit the codebook's creative or ideation task. Experiment II (139 individuals with AI compared with the Experiment I teams) is not randomized and counts only as quasi-experimental context.

one_line_finding: In Experiment I, ChatGPT-4 teams scored higher than human-only teams on judge-rated overall quality (0.417, SE 0.148), novelty (0.344, SE 0.150), and usefulness (0.250, SE 0.150) on a 1-10 scale, N = 244 team-task outputs, with no difference between single- and multiple-AI teams (App. B Tables 1 and 3, pp. 37 and 39).
open_questions: Construct for 'overall quality': coded usefulness because the codebook lists 'quality' there, but it is the paper's overall rating and could be treated as overall_creativity or other.
Assignment is clustered by team, yet all performance regressions use robust (not team-clustered) standard errors with one row per team-task output (two rows per team).

The p. 13 text reports Bayesian estimates for multiple- vs single-AI (Overall -0.072 [-0.303, 0.169]; Novelty 0.025 [-0.220, 0.262]; Usefulness 0.076 [-0.184, 0.323]) that differ from Appendix B Table 4 (-0.024 [-0.273, 0.200]; 0.094 [-0.170, 0.367]; 0.065 [-0.154, 0.296]).
Whether the preregistration (OSF 5su8c) names a primary outcome; it is not in the PDF.
Whether the task type (job-hunting articles and a retail digital-transformation strategy) fits the section's creative-task scope; judges rated novelty, which supports inclusion.
notes: Outcomes left out of the form because they are not creativity scores on the output: task completion time (Tables 7-8), self-reported team process perceptions (coordination, potency, information elaboration, satisfaction; Tables 16-17), and mechanism regressions on prompt length, interaction rounds, and GPT-scored human input (Tables 13-15). Heterogeneity interactions (Table 5) and relative-distribution plots (Figure 5; Appendix B Figures 1-2) are secondary analyses of the same outcomes. Arm SDs in Appendix A Table 1 are at the team-task output level (N = 84/82/78), not the participant level. Small text slips: p. 18 prints 'Novelty (beta = 0.372, p > .05)' while Table 9 marks 0.372 with ** (p < 0.05). Experiment II reuses the Experiment I teams as its comparison groups (same paper, so no cross-paper overlap).
